question: when does the fafsa for the 2026-27 school year open?? i keep seeing different dates
answer: The 2026-27 FAFSA form was available to all applicants by October 1, 2025, and the Department of Education says it launched earlier than in any previous year. It covers the award year that runs from July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027. If you haven't filed yet, you can still do it at StudentAid.gov, but filing as early as possible matters because some state and school aid has early deadlines.

question: Which year's taxes do my parents use on the 2026-27 FAFSA?
answer: The 2026-27 FAFSA uses 2024 tax information, so your parents will need their 2024 federal tax return details, not their most recent one. For most people, that tax information transfers directly from the IRS once each contributor gives consent, so they usually don't have to type it in. If the IRS can't provide it, the contributor may have to enter it manually.

question: What's the actual last day I can submit the 2026-27 FAFSA?
answer: The federal deadline is June 30, 2027: the FAFSA Processing System has to receive your 2026-27 application by that date, and the Department says there are no exceptions. Don't treat that as your real deadline, though. State and college aid deadlines can be much earlier (some states simply say to file as soon as possible after October 1, 2025), and your school needs complete information before your last day of enrollment. Check your state's deadline on StudentAid.gov and ask each school's financial aid office for theirs.

question: My kid's college says priority deadline is in February but the FAFSA site says June. Which one is right?
answer: Both can be right, because they're different deadlines. The federal FAFSA deadline is the last day the Department of Education will accept the form, but states and colleges set their own deadlines for their own aid, and those are often much earlier. Missing a school's priority date can mean missing out on limited funds even if the FAFSA itself is still open. Go by the earliest deadline among your state and the schools on your list.

question: is there a deadline to fix mistakes on my 2026-27 fafsa after i submit it?
answer: Yes. For the 2026-27 award year, electronic and paper corrections, including adding schools or changing an address, must reach the FAFSA Processing System by September 11, 2027. In practice you'll want to fix mistakes much sooner, because your school needs a valid record before it can pay out aid. Make corrections by logging in to your StudentAid.gov account and opening your FAFSA from the dashboard.

question: Does my mom need her own StudentAid.gov account or can she just use mine to fill her part?
answer: She needs her own. Each person who provides information on the online FAFSA form, including parents and spouses, must create their own StudentAid.gov account and should never share login details with anyone. Using someone else's account can cause problems with identity checks and with pulling the right tax information. Your mom can create her account at StudentAid.gov and then complete her section when you invite her.

question: My dad doesn't have a social security number. Can he still do his part of my FAFSA?
answer: Yes. Anyone can create a StudentAid.gov account, even without a Social Security number. A person without an SSN confirms their identity through an extra identity check run by TransUnion, and then they can log in and complete their section online like any other contributor. If he has an ITIN, there's a place to enter it.

question: I made my StudentAid account like an hour ago, should I go ahead and submit my FAFSA now?
answer: It's safer to wait until your account is verified. Accounts made with a Social Security number are matched with the Social Security Administration first, and until that match goes through the Department may not be able to retrieve your federal tax data. The Handbook recommends not signing and submitting the online FAFSA until the account is verified. You can start filling out the form in the meantime and check your account status on StudentAid.gov.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 1: The Application Process: FAFSA to ISIR

question: what even is a 'contributor' on the fafsa? is that someone paying for my school?
answer: No, it has nothing to do with who pays. A contributor is anyone who is required to provide information, consent and approval, and a signature on your FAFSA form. Depending on your situation that can be you, your spouse, your parent, and your parent's spouse or partner. The FAFSA questions decide who your contributors are, and each one completes their part using their own StudentAid.gov account.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 2: Filling Out the FAFSA Form
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 1: The Application Process: FAFSA to ISIR

question: How do I get my parent into my FAFSA so they can fill out their part?
answer: When you fill out the online form, you'll enter your parent's information, including their email address, to invite them. Your parent then gets an email saying they've been invited to contribute to your FAFSA, and they log in with their own StudentAid.gov account to complete their section, give consent and sign. Your FAFSA isn't complete until every required contributor finishes their part, so check your StudentAid.gov dashboard to see where things stand.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 2: Filling Out the FAFSA Form

question: My stepdad says he doesn't want the government looking at his taxes and won't give consent. What happens to my FAFSA?
answer: Every required contributor has to give consent and approval for the Department of Education to get their federal tax information from the IRS. If a required contributor doesn't, the FAFSA is rejected, no Student Aid Index is calculated, and you won't be eligible for federal student aid until that consent is provided. Nobody else can give consent for him, not even a financial aid office. Talk with your school's financial aid office about your situation; they can explain what options, if any, apply to you.

question: My parent doesn't file taxes at all. Do they still have to click the consent thing?
answer: Yes. The FAFSA form says the student and all contributors must provide consent and approval, and that applies whether you file online or on paper. A parent who didn't file taxes still gives consent, and then answers the tax questions as a non-filer. Without consent from everyone required, the student can't receive federal student aid.

question: Can I take back the consent I gave on my FAFSA?
answer: Not for that application year. Once a contributor gives consent and approval for an award year's FAFSA, they cannot revoke it for that cycle. The consent lets the Department get federal tax information directly from the IRS to fill in the financial part of the form. If you have privacy questions, your school's financial aid office or the Federal Student Aid Information Center can explain how that data is used.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 2: Filling Out the FAFSA Form

question: can my school's financial aid counselor give consent for my parents if they're hard to reach?
answer: No. Financial aid administrators, advocates and other helpers are not allowed to provide consent and approval on behalf of a FAFSA contributor. Each contributor has to give it themselves, through their own StudentAid.gov account or by signing the paper form. A counselor can still walk your parents through the steps so they can finish quickly.

question: I'm 20, I work and pay my own rent. Why does the FAFSA still want my parents' info?
answer: The FAFSA decides dependency status by a specific list of questions, not by whether you support yourself. Living apart from your parents or turning 18 or 21 doesn't, on its own, change your status, and even showing that you're fully self-sufficient doesn't count as an unusual circumstance. If none of the independence questions apply to you, you're considered dependent and need a parent's information. If your situation involves something like abandonment or estrangement, talk to your school's financial aid office about a dependency override.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 2: Filling Out the FAFSA Form
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 5: Special Cases

question: what are the questions that make you independent on the 2026-27 fafsa?
answer: For 2026-27 you're independent if at least one of these is true: you were born before January 1, 2003; you're married (not separated); you'll be a graduate or professional student; you're on active duty for purposes other than training, or you're a veteran; you have children or other dependents who get more than half their support from you; at any time since age 13 you were an orphan, a ward of the court or in foster care; you are or were a legally emancipated minor or in a legal guardianship as decided by a court; or on or after July 1, 2025 you were determined to be an unaccompanied homeless youth, or self-supporting and at risk of homelessness. If none apply, you're dependent unless your aid office grants an override for unusual circumstances.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 2: Filling Out the FAFSA Form

question: My parents don't claim me on their taxes anymore. Does that make me independent?
answer: No. Whether your parents claim you on their taxes isn't one of the FAFSA's dependency questions. The Handbook lists it specifically as something that does not qualify as an unusual circumstance for a dependency override. Your status depends on the FAFSA's own questions, like age, marriage, military service, having dependents, or foster care history.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 5: Special Cases

question: What counts as 'unusual circumstances' for getting independent status without parent info?
answer: Unusual circumstances are serious situations that keep you from contacting your parents or getting their information. The Handbook's examples include human trafficking, legally granted refugee or asylum status, parental abandonment or estrangement, parental abuse, and student or parent incarceration. Things that don't qualify include parents refusing to pay for college, parents refusing to fill out the FAFSA, parents not claiming you on taxes, or you being fully self-supporting. Your school's financial aid administrator reviews your situation and decides.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 5: Special Cases

question: im estranged from my parents. how do i fill out the fafsa without them
answer: On the FAFSA, you'll answer the question about unusual circumstances. If you say yes, you can skip the parent section and get a provisional independent status with a provisional Student Aid Index. Your application is then held until the financial aid office at your school reviews it, so contact that office right away and ask what documentation they need, such as a letter from a counselor or other third party. The aid administrator makes the final decision about whether you'll be treated as independent.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 2: Filling Out the FAFSA Form
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 5: Special Cases

question: What does 'provisionally independent' mean on my FAFSA results?
answer: It means you told the FAFSA you have unusual circumstances that prevent you from giving parent information, so the system calculated a provisional SAI without your parents. It's not final: your record stays on hold until a financial aid administrator at your school reviews your situation. The administrator might confirm you as independent, ask for parent information after all, or explain other options. Reach out to your school's aid office and give them what they ask for promptly.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 5: Special Cases

question: If my school approved a dependency override this year, do I have to go through it again next year?
answer: Usually not at the same school. A student whose school granted an override and made a final determination of independence is presumed independent in later award years at that same institution. That changes if your circumstances change or the school has conflicting information. If you transfer to a different school, ask its financial aid office what it needs from you.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 5: Special Cases

question: My parents just refuse to help or fill out the FAFSA. There's no abuse or anything. What can I do?
answer: Parents refusing to help or to provide information doesn't qualify as an unusual circumstance for independence. In that situation, a financial aid administrator may be able to let you receive a Direct Unsubsidized Loan at the dependent student level only. The school will need documentation, ideally a signed statement from your parents saying they won't fill out the FAFSA and won't support you, or a statement from a third party such as a teacher or counselor if they won't sign. Talk with your aid office about this option.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 5: Special Cases
sources.section: Dependent students whose parents refuse to provide support

question: I'm staying with friends and couch surfing since leaving home. Can I be independent on the FAFSA?
answer: You might be. Students under 24 can be considered independent if they're an unaccompanied youth who is homeless, or self-supporting and at risk of being homeless. A financial aid administrator at your school can make that determination, and it can be based on a written statement from you or a documented interview with you. Answer the FAFSA's homelessness questions honestly and contact your school's financial aid office to explain your situation.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 5: Special Cases
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 2: Filling Out the FAFSA Form

question: I live with my grandma and she's my legal guardian. Do I put her info as my parent?
answer: No. For the FAFSA, grandparents, foster parents and legal guardians are not parents unless they've legally adopted you, so their information isn't reported as parent data. However, if a court placed you in a legal guardianship, that is one of the questions that can make you independent. Answer the FAFSA's legal guardianship question accurately, and ask your school's financial aid office if your situation isn't clear.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 2: Filling Out the FAFSA Form
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 2: Filling Out the FAFSA Form

question: what is the SAI exactly and what are the lowest and highest it can be?
answer: The Student Aid Index (SAI) is an eligibility number calculated from your FAFSA answers that schools use to figure out how much need-based aid you can get. For 2026-27 it can range from -1,500 up to 999,999. A lower SAI, including a negative one, means more financial need. It is not a dollar amount of aid and it's not what your family must pay.

sources.title: 2026-27 Student Aid Index (SAI) and Pell Grant Eligibility Guide
Student Aid Index (SAI) Explained

question: My SAI says 9500. Does that mean my family has to pay that much?
answer: No. The SAI is an index that measures financial need, not a bill and not the amount your family is expected to pay. Schools subtract your SAI from their cost of attendance to estimate your financial need, which helps decide how much need-based aid you can get. What you actually pay depends on the school's cost and the aid it offers you, so look at each school's aid offer.

sources.title: Student Aid Index (SAI) Explained
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 3: SAI and Pell Grant Eligibility

question: why is my SAI a negative number? is that an error?
answer: A negative SAI isn't an error. The SAI can go below zero, down to a floor of -1,500, and a negative number signals very high financial need. Some students who qualify for the maximum Pell Grant and who aren't required to file taxes are assigned an SAI of -1,500. You don't need to fix anything unless the answers behind it are wrong.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 3: SAI and Pell Grant Eligibility
2026-27 Student Aid Index (SAI) and Pell Grant Eligibility Guide

question: How do schools actually use my SAI to decide aid?
answer: Each school takes its cost of attendance and subtracts your SAI to estimate your financial need. That need amount helps determine how much need-based aid, like grants and some loans, the school can offer. Because costs differ, the same SAI can mean very different aid at different schools. The school's financial aid office builds your actual aid offer.

sources.title: Student Aid Index (SAI) Explained

question: We have three kids in college next year. Does the FAFSA lower our SAI for that?
answer: Not in the formula anymore. The FAFSA still asks how many people in the family will be in college, but that number is not used to calculate the SAI. Schools can consider it when they look at special circumstances, so it's worth telling each school's financial aid office if several family members are enrolled at the same time.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 2: Filling Out the FAFSA Form

question: I heard there's a new rule where a high SAI means no Pell even if I'd qualify otherwise?
answer: Yes. Starting with 2026-27, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act makes students ineligible for a Pell Grant if their SAI is equal to or greater than twice the maximum Pell Grant award. For 2026-27 the Department set that threshold at an SAI of $14,790. There's an exception for dependents of certain deceased servicemembers and public safety officers. Your school determines Pell eligibility from your FAFSA record, so check your aid offer or ask the aid office.

sources.title: (APP-25-23) 2026-27 FAFSA Form and Pell Grant Eligibility Updates
2026-27 Student Aid Index (SAI) and Pell Grant Eligibility Guide

question: I got something called a FAFSA Submission Summary. What am I supposed to do with it?
answer: The FAFSA Submission Summary shows the answers on your FAFSA, your Student Aid Index, and basic estimates of your eligibility for federal aid. Read it carefully to make sure everything is correct and complete, and make any corrections through your StudentAid.gov account. You can view it online, and a paper copy is mailed if you can't get it online. Your schools get your FAFSA results electronically, and they can't require you to send them the summary to receive aid.

sources.title: 2026-27 FAFSA Form (PDF)
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 1: The Application Process: FAFSA to ISIR

question: I typed the wrong number for something on my FAFSA. How do I fix it?
answer: Log in to StudentAid.gov, go to your dashboard, and open your submitted FAFSA to make a correction, then resubmit it. Corrections are for fixing information that was wrong when you filed. Your school's financial aid office can also submit some corrections for you, but it can't change your personal identifying information or a contributor's consent. Fix errors as soon as you notice them, because your schools get updated results after the correction is processed.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 4: Verification, Updates, and Corrections

question: My dad lost his job after we filed the FAFSA. Can we change the income on it?
answer: Generally no, because the FAFSA isn't updated for information that was correct on the day you signed it, and the income it asks about is from an earlier tax year. Instead, contact the financial aid office at your school and explain the job loss. Aid administrators can use professional judgment to adjust parts of your FAFSA data on a case-by-case basis when you document special circumstances. They'll tell you what paperwork they need.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 4: Verification, Updates, and Corrections
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 5: Special Cases

question: How many colleges can I send my FAFSA to?
answer: You can list up to 20 schools on the online FAFSA, or 10 on the paper form. You can add schools later through StudentAid.gov, or by giving a school's financial aid office your Data Release Number. If you already have 20 school codes on your record, each new school has to replace one of the existing ones.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 2: Filling Out the FAFSA Form
2026-27 FAFSA Form (PDF)

question: I already submitted my FAFSA but forgot a college. Do I have to start over?
answer: No, you don't have to start over. Log in to StudentAid.gov and make a correction to add the school's code, and the school will receive your FAFSA information once it's processed. You can also give the school's financial aid office your Data Release Number so they can add themselves. Do it soon so the school has your information before its deadlines.

sources.title: 2026-27 FAFSA Form (PDF)
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 1: The Application Process: FAFSA to ISIR

question: What does it mean that my FAFSA was 'selected for verification'?
answer: It means your school has to confirm that certain information on your FAFSA is accurate before it can finalize some of your aid. The Department's processing system selects applications, and schools can also choose to verify additional students. Being selected doesn't mean you did anything wrong. Your school's financial aid office will tell you which documents it needs and by when.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 4: Verification, Updates, and Corrections

question: What kind of papers will my school ask for if I'm picked for verification?
answer: It depends on your verification group. Common requests include proof of income, such as an IRS tax return transcript or a signed copy of the tax return, confirmation of family size, and for some students proof of identity. Tax information that came directly from the IRS through the FAFSA is already considered verified, so you usually won't need to document it again. Your school's financial aid office will give you the exact list.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 4: Verification, Updates, and Corrections

question: What happens if I just don't do the verification thing?
answer: If you don't turn in the requested documents by your school's deadline, you lose your Pell Grant eligibility for that award year and must return Pell money already received, and the school can't make additional Direct Loans or pay out more campus-based aid such as FSEOG or Federal Work-Study. For some verification groups, no federal student aid can be paid at all until it's done. If you're struggling to get a document, contact your financial aid office before the deadline.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 4: Verification, Updates, and Corrections

question: Is there a final federal deadline for Pell verification documents for 2026-27?
answer: Yes. For a Pell Grant, your school must receive verification documents by the earlier of 120 days after your last day of enrollment in the 2026-27 award year or September 18, 2027. Your school will usually set its own, earlier deadline, and that's the one to follow. Missing it can cost you the Pell Grant for the year.

sources.title: 2026-2027 Award Year Deadline Dates for the FAFSA Form (Federal Register)

question: Who counts in family size on the FAFSA if I'm a dependent student?
answer: For a dependent student, family size includes you, your parent (and that parent's spouse or partner, if they're included), and your parent's other dependent children who get more than half their support from your parent. It can also include other people who live with your parent and get more than half their support from them. Family size affects the allowances in the SAI formula, so count carefully.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 2: Filling Out the FAFSA Form
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 3: SAI and Pell Grant Eligibility

question: my parents are divorced and i live with my mom most of the time. whose info goes on the fafsa?
answer: The FAFSA uses the parent who provided more financial support to you over the last 12 months, even if that's not the parent you live with most. If neither parent provided more support than the other, use the parent with the greater income and assets. If you're not sure which parent that is, the FAFSA form includes guidance, and your financial aid office can help.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 2: Filling Out the FAFSA Form
2026-27 FAFSA Form (PDF)

question: My mom remarried. Does my stepdad's income go on the FAFSA?
answer: If your mom is the parent whose information goes on the FAFSA, then yes: a stepparent married to that parent counts as a parent and reports their information too. A stepparent who hasn't adopted you can't be the only parent on the form, though. If your other parent is the one who reports, your stepdad's information isn't needed.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 2: Filling Out the FAFSA Form

question: My parents never married but they live together. Do both of them go on the FAFSA?
answer: Yes. Parents who aren't married to each other but live together choose that marital status on the FAFSA, and both of them report their information. Each parent will need to complete their part and give consent through their own StudentAid.gov account.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 2: Filling Out the FAFSA Form

question: Do we have to report our house and my dad's 401k on the FAFSA?
answer: No to both. The home your family lives in isn't reported as an asset, and retirement plans like 401(k)s and pensions aren't either. You do report things like cash, savings and checking, investments, and real estate other than your home. Withdrawals from retirement accounts can still count as income, though.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 2: Filling Out the FAFSA Form
2026-27 FAFSA Form (PDF)

question: My parents own a small family business. Does that count as an asset on the 2026-27 FAFSA?
answer: Starting with 2026-27, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act excludes the net worth of a family-owned business with 100 or fewer full-time or full-time-equivalent employees, so most small family businesses aren't reported. A family business with more than 100 such employees does have to be reported. A commercial fishing business owned and controlled by the family is also excluded. This is a recent change, so check the current FAFSA instructions on StudentAid.gov or ask your financial aid office if you're unsure.

sources.title: (APP-25-23) 2026-27 FAFSA Form and Pell Grant Eligibility Updates
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 2: Filling Out the FAFSA Form

question: We live on our family farm. Do we report the farm's value on the FAFSA?
answer: For the 2026-27 FAFSA, a farm your family lives on is excluded from assets under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, so you don't report its net worth. A farm your family does not live on still has to be reported at its net worth, meaning its current market value minus any debt on it. This rule changed recently, so confirm with the current instructions on StudentAid.gov or with your financial aid office.

sources.title: (APP-25-23) 2026-27 FAFSA Form and Pell Grant Eligibility Updates
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 2: Filling Out the FAFSA Form

question: When I report savings on the FAFSA, do I use what was in the account at the end of last year?
answer: No. Assets are reported as of the day you sign the FAFSA, not as of a past date, so use the current balance or market value on that day. Income is different, since it comes from an earlier tax year.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 2: Filling Out the FAFSA Form
2026-27 FAFSA Form (PDF)

question: Do 529 college savings plans count on the FAFSA for a dependent student?
answer: Yes. 529 college savings plans, the refund value of 529 prepaid tuition plans, and Coverdell accounts count as investments. For a dependent student, an account designated for that student is reported as a parent asset, not a student asset. If you're unsure how a specific account should be reported, ask your financial aid office.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 2: Filling Out the FAFSA Form

question: What are the most common FAFSA mistakes I should watch out for as a first-gen student?
answer: A few to watch for: letting a parent use your StudentAid.gov login instead of their own, forgetting that every contributor must give consent, and reporting the value of your home or retirement accounts when they're excluded. Another common one is assuming you're independent because you live on your own or aren't claimed on taxes. Also, don't wait for the federal deadline when your state and schools may have earlier ones, and respond quickly if your school asks for verification documents.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 1: The Application Process: FAFSA to ISIR
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 2: Filling Out the FAFSA Form
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 4: Verification, Updates, and Corrections

question: My grandparents raised me. Can I just put their info as my parents to make it easier?
answer: No. Grandparents aren't parents for the FAFSA unless they legally adopted you, so their information shouldn't go in the parent section. Reporting the wrong people can delay your aid or force corrections later. Depending on your situation, you may need your parent's information, or you may qualify as independent or for a dependency override, so talk with your school's financial aid office.

question: If I answer unusual circumstances on the FAFSA, will I definitely be independent?
answer: No one can promise that, because the FAFSA answer only gives you a provisional status. The final decision belongs to the financial aid administrator at your school, who reviews your situation and documentation against the federal rules. They may confirm you as independent, ask for parent information, or explain other options. The best step is to contact your aid office early and provide what they ask for.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 5: Special Cases

question: Based on my SAI how much financial aid will I get from my college?
answer: I can't tell you how much you'll get, because your SAI alone doesn't decide that. Each school compares its own cost of attendance with your SAI and then decides what grants, loans and work-study to offer based on federal rules and its own funds. The same SAI can lead to very different offers at different schools. Your school's financial aid office and the aid offer it sends you are where you'll find the real numbers.

sources.title: Student Aid Index (SAI) Explained

question: I'm 22 and fully support myself. Am I eligible to file as independent?
answer: I can't decide your status, but I can explain the rule. Independence on the FAFSA depends on specific questions, such as your birth date, being married, being a graduate student, military service, having dependents, foster care or court-ordered guardianship history, or a homelessness determination. Supporting yourself doesn't, on its own, make you independent. Answer the FAFSA's questions honestly, and if you think something unusual applies, your school's financial aid office decides whether an override is appropriate.

question: If my school picks me for verification will I lose my aid?
answer: Being selected doesn't mean you'll lose aid, and I can't predict your outcome. Verification is a check that your FAFSA information is accurate. If you send everything your school asks for on time, it can finalize your aid, which may change if a correction affects your SAI. If you don't complete it, you can lose Pell Grant and loan eligibility for the year. Your financial aid office makes the decision and can tell you exactly what it needs.
